title: Samadi v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration)
frame:
Forum: Federal Court.
Parties as styled: applicants = FATEMEH SAMADI, HIRAD FOROUTAN AND HIRBOD FOROUTAN; respondent = THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION.
How the layers nest here: The judge is the author (layer 1). The applicant and respondent in this proceeding make submissions to the judge (layer 2). The decision under review was made by an earlier decision-maker (layer 3), and that decision may itself report what a claimant, the Minister or a witness said to that decision-maker (layer 4).

paragraphs.text: Fatemeh Samadi, the principal applicant, is a citizen of Iran. In June 2022, she applied for a work permit under the Start-Up Visa Program. This program is a pathway to permanent residency that allows applicants to apply for a work permit before their application for permanent residency is determined. Ms. Samadi also applied for visitor visas for her two sons – then aged 17 and 15 – so that they could accompany her to Canada.

In three separate decisions all dated May 3, 2024, a visa officer with Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) refused the applications. Ms. Samadi’s application was refused because the officer was not satisfied that the offer of employment supporting her application was genuine and because there was insufficient evidence that significant social, cultural, or economic benefits would accrue from the company’s proposed business activities in Canada. As a result of this refusal, Ms. Samadi’s sons’ applications for visitor visas were also refused.

The applicants have applied for judicial review of these decisions under subsection 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (IRPA). Given that the three decisions are closely connected, the applications for judicial review were ordered consolidated. There is no issue that the judicial reviews of the refusals of visitor visas for Ms. Samadi’s sons stand or fall with the judicial review of the refusal of Ms. Samadi’s work permit.
Ms. Samadi contends that the decision refusing her application for a work permit is unreasonable and that it was made in breach of the requirements of procedural fairness.
As I will explain, I am not persuaded that there is any basis to interfere with the decision. These applications for judicial review will, therefore, be dismissed.

Ms. Samadi is a director and Chief Financial Officer for Vandage Inc, a Canadian-incorporated company developing an innovative technology for adhesive bandages. She holds a Ph.D. in business and financial management and is a member of the faculty of Islamic Azad University in Tehran.

Vandage’s founders are all based in Iran but they want to develop operations in Canada. As stated in correspondence from Ms. Samadi’s authorized representative in support of the visa application: “The goal is to leverage local resources to help grow and succeed in the Canadian healthcare industry by establishing physical presence in Canada. Taking advantage of potential opportunities, developing key partnerships, and accelerating product development will be further enhanced by the move to Canada.” Ms. Samadi in particular was identified by the company as an essential member of the team who for urgent reasons required a work permit before obtaining permanent residence. Her role would be to help start business operations in Canada as soon as possible. Another team member was already in Canada on a work permit when Ms. Samadi’s application was being considered.

When the company was incorporated in Canada, it had four directors (including Ms. Samadi) who were resident in Iran and two non-voting directors who were resident in Canada. It appears that the three other directors of the company besides Ms. Samadi who were resident in Iran also applied for permanent residence in connection with their work with Vandage. There is no other information in the record concerning those applications. In any event, only the refusal of Ms. Samadi’s application for a work permit – and the related applications for visitor visas for her sons – is before me.

The two Canadian-resident directors are Nasser Ashgriz and Mojtaba Falahatinezhad. Mr. Ashgriz is President of UIPatent Corp. and Stokast Inc. while Mr. Falahatinezhad is Vice-President of both companies. UIPatent provides Canadian patent and trademark services for start-up companies; Stokast is an engineering consulting company. Mr. Ashgriz was also named in Vandage’s business plan as part of the advisory team. Vandage had retained UIPatent to prepare and file patent applications on its behalf. The company was also in discussions with Stokast to assist it in the further development of its device in Canada. Vandage had also established a relationship with the Spark Commercialization and Innovation Centre, a start-up business incubator based in Oshawa. The company was also working with the Mila Group, an engineering company in Iran, to build and test its device.

Ms. Samadi’s application for a work permit was initially refused in November 2022 but, after an application for judicial review was commenced, IRCC agreed to reconsider the matter and the judicial review application was discontinued in February 2023.

While the work permit application was pending, in May 2023, the Start Up Visa program requirements were amended to require applicants to establish that the work of their start-up company would create significant economic or social benefits. Previously, it would simply be presumed that such benefits would flow from an entrepreneur establishing a start-up company in Canada. Accordingly, for applications received prior to this change that were still pending, visa officers were directed to request any necessary documents not previously provided so that a complete assessment under this new instruction could be done.

In response to a request from IRCC, Ms. Samadi’s authorized representative submitted updated information in support of the application in July 2023. This information included a progress report for Vandage, which was said to demonstrate “the significant progress the team members have made in Iran.” A covering letter from the authorized representative further explained “in what way the physical presence [in Canada] of the members [of the company] can benefit their business.” The letter stated: “Taking advantage of potential opportunities, developing key partnerships, and accelerating product development will be further enhanced by the move to Canada.” The company’s progress report explained that, to expand its operations in Canada, the company would identify and establish local office space for Vandage’s management team. This local presence will streamline communication and coordination, enabling efficient decision-making and faster progress toward our startup goals. Additionally, we will commence the process of hiring key personnel required to support our activities in Canada, with a focus on finding experts in wound care, product development, and sales.

In March 2024, IRCC sent Ms. Samadi a procedural fairness letter stating that a review of her application had raised concerns that she may not meet the requirements for the work permit she was seeking. Ms. Samadi was therefore asked to provide a number of items of information before a decision was made. The information IRCC requested included statements from the Canadian-resident board members of Vandage – Mr. Ashgriz and Mr. Falahatinezhad – describing their roles in the business, a statement from Ms. Samadi detailing how she became interested in bandages and wound healing, updated information on the supports provided to Vandage by the Spark Centre, evidence of a business bank account in Canada, and evidence of a business operating location in Canada.
Through her representative, Ms. Samadi responded to the procedural fairness letter in April 2024 and provided the information that had been requested.
As noted above, IRCC refused Ms. Samadi’s application on May 3, 2024.

The decision letter states that the application was refused because the visa officer was not satisfied that the offer of employment was genuine and because there was insufficient evidence that significant social, cultural, or economic benefits would accrue from the proposed business activities. The basis for these determinations is set out in the officer’s Global Case Management System (GCMS) notes.

Among the statutory preconditions for issuing a work permit is that the officer must be satisfied that the offer of employment supporting the application is genuine. Under subsection 200(5) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 [IRPR], this determination is based on several factors including whether the offer “is made by an employer that is actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer is made” and whether the offer “is consistent with the reasonable employment needs of the employer.” The officer was not satisfied that these requirements were met.

The officer found that, despite having been incorporated in Canada for over two years, the company was mainly undertaking activities outside Canada and it had done little to establish a solid foundation for itself in Canada. The officer noted in particular that the company did not have a Canadian bank account. Ms. Samadi had explained that this was because the essential team members were all in Iran but the officer did not find this explanation persuasive. One did not have to be a Canadian resident to open a Canadian bank account and, in any event, there was no explanation for why another member of the Vandage team was already in Canada on a work permit or one of the Canadian-resident directors had not opened a bank account. The officer was of the view that the absence of a Canadian bank account suggested that little business activity was actually being conducted in Canada. In sum, the officer found that the company’s main activities were focused outside Canada and a Canadian work permit was not required to conduct those activities.

In addition, paragraph 205(a) of the IRPR provides that a work permit may be issued under section 200 of the IRPR if the work the foreign national intends to perform “would create or maintain significant social, cultural or economic benefits or opportunities for Canadian citizens or permanent residents.” The officer was not satisfied that this was the case.

As already mentioned, the officer found that there was insufficient evidence of the company building a solid business foundation in Canada from which economic benefits in Canada would flow. While the company had some Canadian business links – it had established a relationship with the Spark Centre (the small business incubator) and it had an agreement with UIPatent (the patent and trademark services company) – the officer did not find these links compelling. Despite the relationship with the business incubator, the company’s principals had not taken advantage of any of the services it offered. As well, the one concrete step the company had taken – retaining UIPatent – was of limited significance given that the President of UIPatent, Mr. Ashgriz, is also a director of Vandage. The officer also noted that, while the business plan described plans for the development of a new prototype product, the main activities described in the plan would be taking place outside Canada and in conjunction with a non-Canadian company.
For these reasons, Ms. Samadi’s application for a work permit was refused. As noted above, given this refusal, the visitor visa applications on behalf of her two sons were also refused.
The standards of review are not in dispute.

The parties agree, as do I, that the merits of the officer’s decision should be reviewed on a reasonableness standard (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para 10). A reasonable decision “is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker” (Vavilov, at para 85).

When conducting reasonableness review, a reviewing court must take a “reasons first” approach that examines and evaluates the justification the administrative decision maker has given for its decision, always bearing in mind the history of the proceeding and the administrative context in which the decision was made (Mason v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 SCC 21 at paras 58-60). The reviewing court must read the decision maker’s reasons “holistically and contextually” (Vavilov, at para 97) and in light of “the evidence before the decision maker, the submissions of the parties, publicly available policies or guidelines that informed the decision maker’s work, and past decisions of the relevant administrative body” (Vavilov, at para 94).

To set aside a decision on the basis that it is unreasonable, the reviewing court must be satisfied that “there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency” (Vavilov, at para 100).

To determine whether the requirements of procedural fairness were met, the reviewing court must determine whether the process leading to the decision was fair in all the circumstances (Canadian Pacific Railway Co v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 at paras 54-56; Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness) v Rodas Tejeda, 2026 FCA 115 at para 38). Although, strictly speaking, no standard of review is being applied, this inquiry is functionally the same as applying a correctness standard (Canadian Pacific Railway Co, at para 54; Rodas Tejeda, at paras 38-43). In the present case, the determinative issues are whether Ms. Samadi knew the case she had to meet to establish her eligibility for a work permit and whether she had a full and fair chance to meet that case. V. ANALYSIS A. Was the decision-making process unfair?

Ms. Samadi submits that the requirements of procedural fairness were not met because, while the officer issued a procedural fairness letter, the letter did not communicate the officer’s concerns clearly and, as a result, she did not have a full and fair chance to meet those concerns.

I agree with Ms. Samadi that the adequacy of the procedural fairness letter should be assessed functionally. To serve its intended purpose, the letter must communicate the decision maker’s concerns with sufficient clarity and particularity such that Ms. Samadi (or her representative) had a full and fair opportunity to meet those concerns: see Le v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2025 FC 1965 at para 20, and the cases cited therein. I also agree that the concern expressed in the procedural fairness letter was somewhat generic – that Ms. Samadi “may not meet the requirements of the work permit” she was seeking. I do not agree, however, that the requirements of procedural fairness were not met.

Strictly speaking, since the officer’s concerns related solely to the insufficiency of the application materials in light of the statutory and program requirements, a procedural fairness letter may not even have been necessary: see Lv v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 935 at paras 22-23. Nevertheless, with the officer having seen fit to give Ms. Samadi an opportunity to provide additional information to support her application, I am satisfied that the procedural fairness letter served its intended purpose.

The letter did not simply state a general concern that the application materials previously submitted may be insufficient. It also listed several specific items of information that were relevant to the company’s operations – both past and future – in Canada. I agree with the respondent that the officer’s underlying concern – that there was limited information about the company’s level of involvement in Canada – would be readily apparent from the specific items of information that were requested, even if this was not stated expressly in the letter. The information Ms. Samadi’s representative provided in response addressed this concern. If that information fell short of meeting the officer’s concerns, this was because of the nature of the information provided; it was not because of any deficiency in the procedural fairness letter. While not necessarily determinative, I would also note that there is no evidence that Ms. Samadi’s representative – or Ms. Samadi, for that matter – did not understand what the officer was looking for or why that information would be of interest to the officer.

In sum, having had the benefit of the procedural fairness letter and the opportunity to provide additional information to the decision maker, I am satisfied that Ms. Samadi knew the case she had to meet and had a full and fair opportunity to meet that case.

Ms. Samadi submits that the decision is unreasonable because the officer failed to assess the application in light of all the available information. Instead of recognizing that the development of a start-up company like Vandage must proceed in stages, including work outside Canada, the officer focused unduly on the absence of meaningful work – or plans for work – being undertaken in Canada. In this regard, according to Ms. Samadi, the officer gave undue importance to a relatively insignificant fact – the lack of a Canadian bank account. The officer also unreasonably diminished the significance of the established business relationships in Canada.
I am unable to agree.

It is apparent from their detailed reasons that the officer considered the materials in support of the application carefully and thoroughly. The officer’s reasons for concluding that the materials were insufficient to meet the statutory and program requirements are expressed clearly and intelligibly in the GCMS notes and those reasons justify the final result. In my view, it was not unreasonable for the officer to consider the absence of a Canadian bank account to be evidence of the absence of significant business activity in Canada. Nor was it unreasonable for the officer to give limited weight to the contract with UIPatent given Mr. Ashgriz’s role in both companies. Notably, the retainer for UIPatent was the only concrete step Vandage had taken to establish business relationships in Canada. Even apart from the officer’s concerns about self-dealing (which were reasonable), this can only be described as a modest step from which few economic benefits to Canada could reasonably be said to have flowed. Ms. Samadi has not suggested that the officer has overlooked other significant business relationships. Nor could she given that the relationships with the other Canadian entities identified in the application – the Spark Centre and Stokast – do not appear to have progressed beyond preliminary conversations.

In short, Ms. Samadi has not established that the officer’s reasoning is internally incoherent or that the result is not justified in relation to the constellation of law and facts that are relevant to the decision. While Ms. Samadi understandably disagrees with the officer’s assessment of the business plan and other information, she has not established that that assessment is unreasonable.
For the foregoing reasons, the application for judicial review is dismissed.

The parties did not suggest any serious questions of general importance for certification under paragraph 74(d) of the IRPA. I agree that no question arises. JUDGMENT IN IMM-10402-24 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that The application for judicial review is dismissed. No question of general importance is stated.
